memory_update.text: AI theme should be treated as a capital-intensive system linking hyperscaler demand, accelerator supply, HBM/packaging, networking, data-center infrastructure, power/grid, and enterprise automation monetization.

HBM plus advanced packaging is a high-priority chokepoint candidate because it gates accelerator availability and requires specialized capacity, long qualification cycles, and coordination across memory, foundry, substrate, and equipment suppliers.

Power, cooling, and grid interconnection deserve equal or higher priority than semiconductors in later AI infrastructure research because AI data centers can exceed 100 MW and require scarce electrical equipment and permitting.

Enterprise AI software should be evaluated through monetization evidence such as AI ARR, paid seats, consumption units, renewal rates, automation ROI, and governance adoption rather than generic AI product announcements.

Need Layer 1B/2 work to build a global public-company universe of at least 20 to 40 names across semiconductor, infrastructure, power, and software nodes, then compare evidence strength and market pricing.

layer1a.summary: AI should be decomposed as a multi-layer capital cycle rather than a single semiconductor trade: hyperscaler and enterprise AI demand is pulling on accelerators, HBM, advanced packaging, networking, data-center power/cooling, grid interconnection, and enterprise automation software. The first-pass Serenity framing is that the highest-quality research paths are likely where demand is measurable, expansion is physically or technically constrained, and public-market assets can be tied to hard evidence such as capex, revenue mix, capacity plans, customer wins, qualification cycles, and power interconnection backlogs. This is research support only, not a buy/sell recommendation.

demand_drivers: Hyperscaler AI infrastructure capex for model training, inference, cloud AI services, and internal recommendation/advertising systems.
Enterprise migration from AI pilots to workflow automation, AI agents, software development automation, customer service, cybersecurity, data governance, and industrial/defense use cases.
Custom silicon and networking demand from hyperscalers seeking lower cost, better performance-per-watt, and supply diversification versus merchant GPU dependence.
Inference growth as AI moves from training clusters into search, productivity suites, commerce, coding, media generation, and edge/sovereign deployments.
Power-density growth inside AI data centers, driving demand for liquid cooling, high-voltage electrical gear, UPS, switchgear, transformers, grid services, and contracted clean/baseload power.
theme_map.public_market_search_strategy: Start with the broad AI demand pool, then map public companies by scarce supply-chain node rather than ticker popularity. For each node, search official filings, earnings releases, capex guidance, capacity expansion announcements, customer disclosures, utility/grid filings, equipment order commentary, and segment revenue. Initial screens should include US, Taiwan, Korea, Japan, Europe, and Canadian assets across accelerators, foundry, memory, semiconductor equipment, networking, optical components, electrical infrastructure, utilities, nuclear fuel, cloud platforms, and enterprise automation software. Avoid ranking securities until Layer 1B/2 evidence checks compare bottleneck strength, valuation pressure, and falsification signals.
supply_side_constraints: Advanced-node foundry capacity, EUV tool availability, yield learning, and customer allocation for AI accelerators and custom ASICs.
HBM supply, TSV stacking, advanced DRAM wafer allocation, substrate availability, and memory qualification with accelerator platforms.
Advanced packaging capacity such as CoWoS, SoIC, interposers, substrates, thermal materials, and packaging equipment throughput.
AI networking fabric constraints including high-speed switch ASICs, optics, SerDes, cables, Ethernet/InfiniBand ecosystem qualification, and cluster-scale reliability.
Data-center power availability, interconnection queues, local permitting, transformers, switchgear lead times, cooling infrastructure, land, water, and construction labor.
Software monetization uncertainty: agent adoption can be rapid, but ROI, data readiness, governance, security, and workflow integration remain gating factors.
